newsitem.title: USA: Securities ligitation reform bill expected soon.
newsitem.headline: Securities ligitation reform bill expected soon.

text.p: A heated debate in Congress about curtailing investor lawsuits against companies and their advisers may soon erupt, slightly more than a year after massive reforms were enacted over President Clinton's veto.

Lawmakers are expected to propose legislation in the House of Representatives in the coming weeks that would stop securities class action suits from migrating to state courts, congressional aides and industry officials say.

The controversial securities litigation reform, which was passed over a presidential veto in late 1995, is designed to reduce the amount of meritless cases in federal courts by, among other things, raising the qualifying standards.
Opponents include consumer groups which warn that the new standards leave investors with little legal recourse, even when companies and their executives make misleading forecasts.
The legislation is to be introduced by Democratic Representative Anna Eshoo of California and Republican Representative Rick White of Washington, Congressional aides said Tuesday.

The details of the measure, and how broad it will reach, were still not clear, the aides said. But its intent will be to stop litigators from using state courts to get around federal reforms passed by Congress in 1995.
"It just seems that we fixed this at one level but I think folks have found a way around the fix and that is through the state courts," an aide to White said.

The legislation has been sought by the Uniform Standards Coalition, a nationwide organisation of high-tech companies, venture capitalists and others who are seeking Congressional action to put an end to what they call frivolous lawsuits.
"What we've been doing is working with people on the Hill to put together some legislation that would create uniform standards," coalition executive director Mark Gitenstein said.
"The same set of rules ought to apply to federal litigation as to state litigation," he added.
The group, which spent millions to fight a ballot initiative in California it said would have undermined Congress' reforms, is now focusing on Washington.

The high-tech industry coalition claims that a small group of lawyers that specialises in securities class action suits has evaded the 1995 reforms by shifting cases to state courts, where the qualifying standards are lower.
The group says this is a costly and risky development for start-up companies that want to avoid litigation.
"We're trying to fill that loophole, nothing more nothing less," Gitenstein said.
But their concerns, which have been taken up by some 60 House Democrats, including Eshoo, have received a lukewarm response from the White House.
"My Administration will be reviewing the SEC study and other reports and data to assess the need for further action," Clinton wrote in an April 25 letter to Eshoo.
